title: Psalm 72: Endow the King with Your Justice
summary: A prayer for the king asks God to give him justice and righteousness so that he will defend the poor, crush the oppressor, and bring peace and plenty to the land. It prays that his rule will reach from sea to sea, that distant kings will bring him gifts, and that all nations will be blessed in him. A doxology blessing the LORD closes Book II of the Psalms, followed by a note that the prayers of David are concluded.
story: Psalm 72 closes Book II of the Psalter (Psalms 42 to 72), just as Psalm 41 closed Book I. After many laments of a king under pressure, the book ends with a prayer for what the king is meant to be. It takes the promises God made to David, that his son would have an enduring throne (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18), and turns them into a prayer. The following books of the Psalter will trace what happened when the Davidic kings failed, culminating in the lament over the broken covenant in Psalm 89 at the end of Book III. Psalm 72 is the high-water mark of royal hope.
historical:
The heading reads simply “Of Solomon”, one of only two psalms attributed to him (the other is Psalm 127). The Hebrew preposition can mean by, for, or concerning Solomon, and interpreters read it all three ways. Some see it as Solomon's own prayer at the start of his reign, echoing his request for wisdom to judge God's people (1 Kings 3:9). Others take it as David's prayer for his son, which fits the closing note in verse 20 about the prayers of David, and the Septuagint heading, which can be read as for Solomon. Many modern scholars see it as a coronation or royal psalm used for Davidic kings more generally, perhaps at an enthronement, with Solomon's name attached because his reign became the model of peace and wealth.

Verse 20 raises its own question. It says the prayers of David son of Jesse are concluded, yet more psalms of David appear later (for example Psalms 86, 101, 103, 108 to 110, and 138 to 145). Most scholars take the verse as the ending note of an earlier collection of Davidic prayers that was later incorporated into the larger Psalter, where the note was kept even though more Davidic psalms were added afterward.
cultural:
Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to guarantee justice for the weak. Royal inscriptions and law codes, like the prologue and epilogue framing Hammurabi's laws in Babylon, present the king as the protector of the widow and the orphan. Israel shared that ideal but grounded it in God's own justice: the king was to receive his justice from God and to exercise it on God's behalf. The prayers for rain on mown grass (verse 6) and grain waving on the hilltops (verse 16) reflect the common belief that a righteous reign brought fertility and prosperity to the land.

The geography of verses 8 to 10 sketches the known world as Israel saw it. The Euphrates was the great river of Mesopotamia and the traditional northern boundary of the promised land. Tarshish was a distant port in the west, possibly in Spain, though its location is debated. Sheba lay in southern Arabia and was famous for gold, spices, and incense, and its queen visited Solomon (1 Kings 10). Seba is less certain; many place it in Africa, near Cush. The picture is of tribute flowing to Jerusalem from every horizon, as it did briefly in Solomon's day.
literary: The psalm is almost entirely a series of wishes, “May he” and “May they”, a kind of royal blessing. It moves in waves: justice for the poor (verses 1 to 4), long life and fruitful reign (verses 5 to 7), worldwide dominion (verses 8 to 11), the reason for it all, compassion for the needy (verses 12 to 14), and prosperity and blessing (verses 15 to 17). The center of the psalm, verses 12 to 14, gives the ground of the king's greatness: he rescues the needy, and their blood is precious in his sight. Verses 18 and 19 are a doxology, a formal blessing of God that marks the end of Book II, and verse 20 is an editorial note rather than part of the poem.

outline.t: Justice and righteousness for the afflicted
The king who rescues the needy
Prosperity and blessing for all nations

doctrines.note: The psalm pictures God's rule exercised through a human king whose reign brings justice, peace, and plenty to the whole earth. It is a portrait of what God's kingdom looks like when it comes in full.

Although it was a prayer for Israel's kings, its hopes (endless reign, worldwide rule, blessing to all nations) went far beyond any historical king. Jewish and Christian readers came to read it as a picture of the Messiah, the anointed king to come.
The psalm weaves together God's covenant with David and his promise to Abraham. Verse 17, praying that all nations be blessed in the king, echoes Genesis 12:3.

words.note: Mishpat, justice. It means the right ordering of relationships, especially the protection of those who cannot protect themselves. In verse 1 justice is God's gift to the king; he cannot produce it himself.

Ebyon, needy. It appears four times in the psalm. The king's worth is measured by how he treats those with the least power. In verses 12 to 14 his care for the needy is the reason the nations should honor him.
Shalom, peace or well-being. In verses 3 and 7 it means more than the absence of war: it is flourishing, prosperity, and wholeness for the community. A just king makes the land itself yield peace.

christ: No Davidic king fulfilled this psalm; even Solomon, whose reign came closest, ended in idolatry and a divided kingdom. The psalm's hopes therefore pointed beyond history toward a king still to come. The Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms known as the Targum reads the king in verse 1 as the Messiah, and Christians have read it of Jesus. Matthew's account of wise men bringing gold and frankincense from the east (Matthew 2:11) echoes the gifts of distant kings in verses 10 and 15, and the hope that all nations be blessed in the king (verse 17) is the promise to Abraham that Paul says is fulfilled in Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16). Jesus announced good news to the poor and gave himself for the needy, and the New Testament looks for the day when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (Revelation 11:15). Isaac Watts's hymn Jesus Shall Reign is a paraphrase of this psalm.
questions: The psalm measures the king's greatness by how he treats the poor and needy. How would that standard change the way we evaluate leaders, including ourselves?
Verse 14 says the blood of the oppressed is precious in the king's sight. Who in your community is treated as if their life were cheap?
The psalm prayed for a king who never fully came in Israel's history. How does it shape your hope for Christ's kingdom?
